title: Two Sum
statement: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers that add up to target. Each input has exactly one solution.
hints: A brute-force double loop works but is O(n^2) - can you do better?
As you scan, what would you need to remember to check each number instantly?
Store each value's index in a hash map; for x, look up (target - x).
approach: One pass: for each x, check if complement exists in the map; else store x. Guaranteed one solution.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
statement: Given prices where prices[i] is the day-i price, pick one day to buy and a later day to sell for maximum profit. Return 0 if no profit possible.
hints: Track the lowest price seen so far as you go.
At each day, the best profit ending today = price - min_price_so_far.
Keep a running maximum of that value.
approach: Single left-to-right scan maintaining min_price and max_profit.

title: Maximum Subarray
statement: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum and return that sum.
hints: Decide at each element: extend the previous subarray or start fresh here.
Keep two numbers: best sum ending at i, and best sum seen anywhere.
This is Kadane's algorithm.
approach: Iterate once; cur = max(x, cur + x); best = max(best, cur).
pitfalls: Resetting cur to 0 breaks all-negative arrays

title: Product of Array Except Self
statement: Given nums, return an array where answer[i] is the product of all elements except nums[i]. No division; O(n) time.
hints: The answer for i = (product of left part) x (product of right part).
Compute left products in a forward pass into the output array.
Then sweep backward multiplying in the right products - O(1) extra space.
approach: Two passes: prefix products into output, then suffix product accumulated backward.
complexity: Time O(n), Space O(1) excluding output
pitfalls: Extra arrays when O(1) space is required

title: 3Sum
statement: Find all unique triplets [a,b,c] in nums with a+b+c = 0.
hints: Sorting first makes duplicates manageable - why?
Fix one element, then use two pointers on the rest like Two Sum II.
Skip equal neighbors after sorting to avoid duplicate triplets.
approach: Sort; for each i, two-pointer scan of (i+1..end); skip duplicates at all three positions.
complexity: Time O(n^2), Space O(1) excluding output

title: Container With Most Water
statement: Given heights, find two lines forming the container holding the most water.
hints: Start with the widest container (both ends) and narrow it.
Which pointer should move - and why is it safe to move it?
Move the shorter side: it can never form a better pair at this width.
approach: Two pointers inward; area = min(h[l],h[r]) * (r-l); move the smaller height.
pitfalls: Moving the taller pointer (loses the proof)

title: Trapping Rain Water
statement: Given an elevation map, compute how much water it traps after raining.
hints: Water at i = min(tallest left, tallest right) - height[i].
Precompute left-max and right-max arrays for an O(n) space solution.
Two pointers can do it in O(1) space: always advance the lower side.
approach: Two pointers with left_max/right_max; add water on the lower side each step.

title: Find the Duplicate Number
statement: Array of n+1 integers in [1, n] with one duplicate. Find it without modifying the array, O(1) space.
hints: Treat values as next-pointers: index i -> nums[i] forms a linked list with a cycle.
The duplicate is the cycle entrance (two numbers point to it).
Apply Floyd's tortoise and hare, then find the entrance.
approach: Phase 1: find meeting point. Phase 2: one pointer to start, move both - they meet at the duplicate.
pitfalls: Binary-search-on-count is O(n log n) - acceptable but not the intended trick

title: First Missing Positive
statement: Find the smallest missing positive integer in an unsorted array. O(n) time, O(1) space.
hints: The answer is in [1, n+1] - so ignore everything else.
Place each x in [1,n] at index x-1 by swapping (cyclic sort).
Then the first index i with nums[i] != i+1 gives the answer.
approach: Cyclic placement pass, then a linear scan for the first misplaced value.
pitfalls: Infinite swap loops (skip when already correct)

title: Merge Intervals
statement: Merge all overlapping intervals.
hints: What order makes overlaps easy to detect? Sort by start.
Keep a 'current' interval; extend its end or start a new one.
Touching intervals like [1,4],[4,5]: decide merge per the problem's definition.
approach: Sort by start; sweep, merging into the current interval when overlapping.
complexity: Time O(n log n), Space O(1) excluding output

title: Rotate Array
statement: Rotate the array right by k steps, in place.
hints: Reversing is its own inverse - how can three reverses rotate?
Reverse all, then reverse the first k, then the rest.
Remember k %= n first.
approach: k %= n; reverse(0,n); reverse(0,k); reverse(k,n).
pitfalls: Forgetting k %= n (k can exceed n)

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
statement: Count the number of contiguous subarrays summing to k.
hints: If you knew all prefix sums, when does a subarray sum to k?
prefix[j] - prefix[i] = k  =>  look up (prefix[j] - k) seen before.
Seed the map with {0: 1} for subarrays starting at index 0.
approach: Running prefix sum; add map.get(prefix - k, 0) to the count; then record prefix.

title: Valid Anagram
statement: Determine if string t is an anagram of string s.
hints: Anagrams have identical character frequencies.
Count with a 26-array (lowercase) or a hash map for Unicode.
Early exit when lengths differ.
approach: Build frequency counts for s, decrement for t; all zeros (or use Counter).
complexity: Time O(n), Space O(1) for fixed alphabet
pitfalls: Sorting is O(n log n) - fine but slower

title: Group Anagrams
statement: Group an array of strings into anagram groups.
hints: Anagrams share a canonical key - what could it be?
Sorted string, or a 26-count tuple (avoids O(k log k) sort).
Map key -> list; return the values.
approach: Hash map keyed by character-count tuple; append each string to its group.
pitfalls: Using the sorted string when k is huge

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
statement: Length of the longest substring with all distinct characters.
hints: Grow the right edge; when a duplicate appears, jump the left edge past its last occurrence.
A last-seen index map makes the jump O(1).
left = max(left, last_seen[ch] + 1) - never move left backward.
approach: Sliding window with a last-occurrence map; track max window size.
pitfalls: Moving left to last_seen+1 without max() (moves backward)

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
statement: Return the longest palindromic substring of s.
hints: Every palindrome has a center - expand around each of the 2n-1 centers.
Even and odd lengths need separate centers.
Manacher's O(n) exists; expand-around-center O(n^2) is the expected answer.
approach: For each center, expand while s[l]==s[r]; keep the longest.

title: Minimum Window Substring
statement: Smallest substring of s containing all characters of t (with frequencies).
hints: Expand right until the window is valid; then shrink left while it stays valid.
Track 'formed' = how many distinct chars meet their required count.
Record the best window during shrinking.
approach: Sliding window with need-counts and a formed counter; shrink greedily.
pitfalls: Shrinking before the window is valid
Not handling duplicate chars in t

title: Valid Parentheses
statement: Determine if a bracket string is valid (properly closed and nested).
hints: Open brackets go on a stack; closers must match the top.
A closer with an empty stack, or leftover opens at the end, means invalid.
Map closer -> opener for clean matching.
approach: Stack scan; push opens, pop-and-check on closers; valid iff stack empty at end.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
statement: Longest substring with same letter after at most k replacements.
hints: In a window, replacements needed = window_size - max_frequency.
Keep the window valid (replacements <= k); max_freq never decreases - why is that OK?
Because we only care about the maximum window seen.
approach: Sliding window tracking max char frequency; shrink when window - maxfreq > k.

title: Encode and Decode Strings
statement: Design an encoding of a string list to a single string and back (strings may contain any chars).
hints: Delimiters can appear in the data - so prefix each string with its length.
Format: '<len>#<string>' repeated; decode by reading the length first.
Why does this handle every edge case?
approach: Length-prefix encoding; decode by parsing '<digits>#', then slicing exactly len chars.
pitfalls: Using a separator character (breaks on data containing it)

title: Reverse Linked List
statement: Reverse a singly linked list iteratively and recursively.
hints: You need three pointers: prev, curr, and a temp for next.
At each step: save next, flip curr.next to prev, advance.
Recursive: reverse the rest, then fix the two links at the front.
approach: Iterative three-pointer loop; recursive trust-the-subproblem.
complexity: Time O(n), Space O(1) iterative / O(n) recursive
pitfalls: Losing the next pointer before flipping

title: Linked List Cycle II (find cycle start)
statement: Detect whether a linked list has a cycle; if so return the node where it begins.
hints: Floyd: slow (+1) and fast (+2); meeting means a cycle.
Why does resetting one pointer to head and advancing both find the entrance?
Distance math: they meet k steps before the entrance along the cycle.
approach: Phase 1 meet; phase 2 reset slow to head, advance both one step - meeting node is the entrance.
pitfalls: Returning the meeting point as the answer (wrong)
Hash set works but uses O(n) space

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
statement: Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list.
hints: A dummy head removes the special case for the first node.
Always attach the smaller head and advance it.
Recursive version is a clean 5-liner.
approach: Dummy head; iterative attach-smaller; or recursion.

title: Remove Nth Node From End
statement: Remove the nth node from the end in one pass.
hints: Two pointers n apart: when the front hits the end, the back is at the target's predecessor.
A dummy head handles n == length (removing the head).
Count the gap carefully: front starts n steps ahead.
approach: Dummy head; advance fast n+1 steps; move both; delete slow.next.
pitfalls: Crash when removing the head without dummy

title: Reorder List
statement: Reorder L0->L1->...->Ln into L0->Ln->L1->Ln-1->...
hints: Split the list in half (slow/fast).
Reverse the second half.
Merge the two halves alternately.
approach: Three composed subproblems; all O(1) space.
pitfalls: Wrong split point on odd lengths

title: Add Two Numbers
statement: Two numbers as reverse-order linked lists; return their sum as a list.
hints: Add digit by digit with a carry, like grade-school addition.
Lists may differ in length; a final carry may add a node.
Dummy head again simplifies everything.
approach: Walk both lists with carry; append (total % 10); carry = total // 10.
complexity: Time O(max(n,m)), Space O(max(n,m)) for output

title: Copy List with Random Pointer
statement: Deep-copy a list where each node has next and random pointers.
hints: A map from old node to new node solves it in two passes.
Can you do O(1) space? Interleave copies: A->A'->B->B'.
Then wire A'.random = A.random.next, and finally split the lists.
approach: Hash-map version for clarity; interleave trick for O(1) space.
complexity: Time O(n), Space O(n) map / O(1) interleave
pitfalls: Breaking the original list during split

title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
statement: Reverse the list k nodes at a time; leave the remainder as-is.
hints: Process group by group: reverse k, connect to the next group's result.
First check that k nodes remain; if not, leave them.
Recursion handles 'the rest' elegantly.
approach: Count k nodes; reverse the group; recurse on the remainder; stitch.

title: Palindrome Linked List
statement: Determine if a singly linked list is a palindrome, O(1) space.
hints: Find the middle, reverse the second half, compare.
O(n) space via array copy is the easy version - then optimize.
Optionally restore the list afterward.
approach: Middle via slow/fast; reverse second half; pairwise compare.

title: Merge K Sorted Lists
statement: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted list.
hints: Merging pairwise is O(kN); a heap of k heads is better.
Push all heads; repeatedly pop min, push its next.
Divide-and-conquer merging is an O(N log k) alternative.
approach: Min-heap over current heads; pop/push until empty.
complexity: Time O(N log k), Space O(k)
pitfalls: Forgetting to push next after pop

title: Min Stack
statement: Stack supporting push, pop, top, and getMin in O(1).
hints: Each stack entry can remember the minimum below it.
Store pairs (value, min_so_far), or keep a parallel min-stack.
Duplicate minimums must be handled - think about pop logic.
approach: Auxiliary min tracking per element; getMin reads the top's stored min.
complexity: Time O(1) all ops, Space O(n)
pitfalls: Popping the min tracking on duplicate mins

title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
statement: Evaluate an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation.
hints: Numbers go on the stack; operators pop two operands.
Order matters for - and /: second-popped is the left operand.
Integer division truncates toward zero.
approach: Stack scan; apply operators to the top two values.

title: Daily Temperatures
statement: For each day, how many days until a warmer temperature (0 if none).
hints: A decreasing stack of indices holds days awaiting a warmer day.
When today is warmer than the stack top, resolve those days: answer = i - idx.
Each index is pushed and popped once.
approach: Monotonic decreasing stack; resolve on warmer days.
pitfalls: Using temperatures instead of indices (need distances)

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
statement: Largest rectangle area in a histogram.
hints: A bar's max rectangle extends until a smaller bar on each side.
Increasing stack: when a smaller bar arrives, pop and compute areas.
A sentinel zero bar flushes the stack at the end.
approach: Monotonic increasing stack with sentinel; area = height * width on pop.
pitfalls: Width miscalculation (use current index - stack top - 1)

title: Valid Parentheses (extended: minimum removals)
statement: Given a bracket string, remove the minimum brackets to make it valid.
hints: First pass: mark indices of unmatched closers and leftover opens.
A stack of indices (not chars) makes marking easy.
Rebuild the string skipping marked indices.
approach: Index stack to find unmatched positions; filter them out.

title: Implement Queue using Stacks
statement: Implement a FIFO queue with two LIFO stacks.
hints: One stack for input, one for output; transfer lazily.
Only move elements when the output stack is empty - why?
Amortized O(1): each element moves at most twice.
approach: Push to in-stack; pop/peek transfer to out-stack when empty.

title: Next Greater Element I
statement: For each element in nums1, find its next greater element in nums2 (nums1 subset of nums2).
hints: Process nums2 once with a decreasing stack, recording next-greater in a map.
Then answer each nums1 query by lookup.
Remaining stack elements map to -1.
approach: Monotonic stack over nums2 -> map; O(1) per query.

title: Asteroid Collision
statement: Asteroids move left/right; simulate collisions (larger survives; equal both explode).
hints: Only right-moving asteroids on the stack can collide with an incoming left-mover.
While loop: resolve repeated collisions against the stack top.
Left-movers never collide with each other.
approach: Stack of right-movers; resolve each left-mover against the stack.
pitfalls: Single if instead of while (chain collisions)

title: Simplify Path (Unix)
statement: Canonicalize an absolute Unix path.
hints: Split on '/'; push normal names, pop on '..', ignore '.' and empties.
Join the stack with '/' and prefix '/'.
Multiple slashes collapse naturally via the split.
approach: Stack of path components; handle '..', '.', and empty tokens.

title: Decode String (k[encoded])
statement: Decode strings like '3[a2[c]]' -> 'accaccacc'.
hints: Two stacks: counts and current strings; '[' pushes, ']' resolves.
Multi-digit counts need accumulation before '['.
Recursive descent is equally clean.
approach: Stack-based parse; on ']' pop count and string, repeat and append.

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
statement: Find the maximum depth (longest root-to-leaf path) of a binary tree.
hints: Depth = 1 + max(depth of children).
Base case: null node has depth 0.
BFS level-counting works too.
approach: Recursive: 1 + max(left, right); or iterative BFS counting levels.

title: Invert Binary Tree
statement: Invert a binary tree (mirror it).
hints: At each node, swap left and right children.
Then recurse into both (now-swapped) children.
BFS version: swap as you visit each node.
approach: Post-order swap at every node, recursively or iteratively.
pitfalls: Swapping after recursing into the wrong child

title: Diameter of Binary Tree
statement: Length (edges) of the longest path between any two nodes.
hints: The longest path through a node = left depth + right depth.
Compute depths bottom-up, tracking the max path seen.
Similar to max-depth, with one extra global.
approach: Post-order: return depth, update global max of left+right.
pitfalls: Returning the path instead of its length

title: Balanced Binary Tree
statement: Determine if a binary tree is height-balanced (children's heights differ by at most 1 everywhere).
hints: Naive: check balance at each node with depth calls - O(n^2).
Better: return -1 for unbalanced subtrees in one pass.
Combine depth computation with the balance check.
approach: Post-order returning height or -1 (unbalanced sentinel).

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
statement: Determine if a binary tree is a valid BST.
hints: Each node must lie within (low, high) bounds passed down.
Inorder traversal of a BST is sorted - alternative check.
Duplicates: decide strict vs non-strict per the problem.
approach: DFS with bounds; or inorder with prev-value tracking.
pitfalls: Only comparing with parent (grandparent violations missed)

title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
statement: Find the kth smallest value in a BST.
hints: Inorder traversal visits nodes in sorted order - stop at k.
Iterative with an explicit stack avoids recursion depth issues.
Augmented subtree sizes give O(h) per query.
approach: Inorder counting to k; or order-statistic tree augmentation.
pitfalls: Full traversal when early stop suffices

title: Lowest Common Ancestor (Binary Tree)
statement: Find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes in a binary tree.
hints: If a subtree contains both/neither/one, what should it return?
Return p or q when found; the first node receiving both is the LCA.
BST version is simpler: walk down by comparisons.
approach: Recursive: combine left/right results; LCA is where both sides are non-null.
pitfalls: Assuming BST properties in a general tree

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
statement: Return node values grouped by depth level.
hints: BFS; capture queue size at each level to group nodes.
DFS with a depth parameter also works (append to level list).
Zigzag: alternate the append direction per level.
approach: Queue-based BFS with per-level snapshots.

title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
statement: Design an algorithm to serialize a binary tree to a string and back.
hints: Preorder with '#' markers for nulls captures the full structure.
Deserialize by consuming tokens with an index pointer.
Level-order also works; compare compactness.
approach: Preorder encode with null markers; recursive decode consuming tokens.

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
statement: Maximum sum over all paths (any start/end) in a binary tree.
hints: For each node: best downward path = val + max(0, left, right).
A path THROUGH the node can use both children: candidate = val + left + right.
Return downward-best upward; track the global through-max.
approach: Post-order returning max downward path; global max over through-paths.
pitfalls: Confusing return value with global answer

title: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
statement: Count nodes where the path from root contains no greater value.
hints: Pass the maximum seen so far down the recursion.
A node is good iff node.val >= max_so_far.
Update max_so_far for children.
approach: DFS carrying path maximum; count when node.val >= max.
pitfalls: Using global max instead of path max

title: Construct Tree from Preorder and Inorder
statement: Rebuild a binary tree from its preorder and inorder traversals.
hints: preorder[0] is the root; find it in inorder to split left/right subtrees.
A value->index map makes the split O(1).
Recurse with index ranges, not slices (avoid O(n^2) copying).
approach: Recursive build with (pre_idx, in_left, in_right) ranges and an index map.
pitfalls: Linear search for root in inorder

title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
statement: Find the kth largest element without fully sorting.
hints: A min-heap of size k keeps the k largest; the top is the answer.
Quickselect partitions like quicksort: average O(n).
Compare: heap is simpler, quickselect is faster on average.
approach: Min-heap of size k; or quickselect for average O(n).
complexity: Time O(n log k) heap / O(n) avg quickselect, Space O(k)

title: Top K Frequent Elements
statement: Return the k most frequent elements.
hints: Count frequencies, then either heap (O(n log k)) or bucket by count (O(n)).
Bucket index = frequency; scan buckets from high to low.
Which is better depends on constraints - discuss.
approach: Frequency map + bucket sort by count; or min-heap of size k.
pitfalls: Sorting all frequencies O(n log n)
Forgetting ties can exceed k (fine - return any k)

title: Find Median from Data Stream
statement: Support addNum and findMedian on a stream.
hints: Two heaps: max-heap for the lower half, min-heap for the upper half.
Keep sizes balanced (differ by at most 1); median from the tops.
Every addNum: push, then rebalance.
approach: Dual-heap with size invariant; median is top(s).
complexity: Time O(log n) add, O(1) median; Space O(n)
pitfalls: Python heapq is min-heap: negate for max-heap

title: Task Scheduler
statement: Minimum intervals to run tasks with cooldown n between same tasks.
hints: The most frequent task dictates the skeleton: (maxFreq-1) * (n+1) slots.
Add the count of tasks tied for max frequency.
Take max with total tasks (no idle needed if dense).
approach: Frequency formula; or greedy simulation with max-heap + cooldown queue.

title: K Closest Points to Origin
statement: Return the k closest points to (0,0).
hints: Compare squared distances (skip sqrt).
Max-heap of size k, or quickselect on distance.
Sorting all is O(n log n) - beatable.
approach: Max-heap of size k by squared distance; or quickselect.
complexity: Time O(n log k), Space O(k)

title: IPO (maximize capital with k projects)
statement: Pick up to k projects to maximize final capital; each needs min capital and yields profit.
hints: Sort projects by required capital; use a max-heap for affordable profits.
Each round: move newly-affordable projects into the heap, take the best.
Greedy works because profits only increase affordability.
approach: Sort by capital + max-heap of profits; k rounds.
complexity: Time O(n log n), Space O(n)
pitfalls: Re-scanning affordable projects each round O(kn)
Taking projects in requirement order only

title: Sliding Window Maximum
statement: Maximum of each sliding window of size k.
hints: A decreasing deque of indices gives O(n): front is always the max.
Evict indices outside the window from the front.
Heap with lazy deletion is O(n log k) - acceptable alternative.
approach: Monotonic deque; maintain decreasing values, drop out-of-window.
pitfalls: Heap without lazy deletion of stale entries

title: Meeting Rooms II (min conference rooms)
statement: Minimum rooms so all meetings fit.
hints: Sort by start; a min-heap of end times tracks busy rooms.
If the earliest-ending room frees before this starts, reuse it.
Heap size at the end = answer.
approach: Sweep line with min-heap of end times.
complexity: Time O(n log n), Space O(n)

title: Number of Islands
statement: Count the islands (connected '1's, 4-directional) in a binary grid.
hints: Each unvisited '1' starts a new island - flood-fill it.
Mark visited by flipping to '0' (in-place) or a visited set.
DFS recursive or BFS iterative both work.
approach: Scan grid; on unvisited '1', increment count and flood-fill its region.
complexity: Time O(mn), Space O(mn) worst-case recursion

title: Clone Graph
statement: Deep-copy a connected undirected graph given a reference node.
hints: A map from original node to clone handles cycles.
DFS: clone node, then recursively clone neighbors.
BFS version is equally valid.
approach: DFS/BFS with old->new map; wire neighbors to clones.
pitfalls: Infinite recursion on cycles (no map check)

title: Course Schedule
statement: Can you finish n courses given [course, prerequisite] pairs?
hints: Model as a directed graph; the question is cycle detection.
Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove zero-indegree nodes.
If all nodes are removed, no cycle exists.
approach: Build adjacency + indegree; BFS from zero-indegree nodes; check count.
pitfalls: DFS color method: forgetting the 'visiting' state

title: Course Schedule II (return ordering)
statement: Return a valid course order, or empty array if impossible.
hints: Same as Course Schedule, but record the removal order.
That order IS a valid topological ordering.
Any valid order is accepted.
approach: Kahn's algorithm recording the dequeue order.
pitfalls: Returning partial order on cycle (must return [])

title: Rotting Oranges
statement: Minutes until no fresh orange remains (4-directional spread per minute); -1 if impossible.
hints: Multi-source BFS: enqueue ALL rotten oranges at time 0.
Level-order traversal counts minutes.
Count fresh oranges; leftovers mean -1.
approach: BFS from all rotten sources simultaneously; levels = minutes.
pitfalls: BFS from each rotten separately (wrong timing)

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
statement: Cells with heights; find cells from which water flows to both oceans (borders).
hints: Forward simulation from every cell is O((mn)^2) - reverse it.
Start BFS/DFS from each ocean's border, moving to equal-or-higher cells.
Intersect the two reachable sets.
approach: Two reverse flood-fills from ocean borders; intersect reachable cells.
pitfalls: Wrong flow direction (must go uphill in reverse)

title: Graph Valid Tree
statement: Given n nodes and edges, determine if they form a valid tree.
hints: A tree: exactly n-1 edges AND connected (either implies the other given no self-loops... check both).
Union-Find: any union of already-connected nodes means a cycle.
Or DFS: no cycles and visit count == n.
approach: Check edge count, then Union-Find for cycles / connectivity.

title: Number of Connected Components
statement: Count connected components in an undirected graph.
hints: Union all edges; count distinct roots.
Or DFS/BFS from each unvisited node, counting launches.
Isolated nodes count as their own component.
approach: Union-Find over edges; count unique parents.

title: Word Ladder
statement: Shortest transformation sequence length from beginWord to endWord, changing one letter at a time through valid words.
hints: Model words as a graph; BFS gives the shortest path.
Neighbors via wildcard patterns (*ot -> hot, dot) precomputed in a map.
Bidirectional BFS halves the search.
approach: BFS with pattern-bucket adjacency; bidirectional for speed.
complexity: Time O(n * L^2), Space O(n * L)
pitfalls: Rebuilding neighbors by scanning all words each time

title: Network Delay Time (Dijkstra)
statement: Time for a signal from node k to reach all nodes (directed weighted edges); -1 if unreachable.
hints: Classic single-source shortest path with non-negative weights: Dijkstra.
Heap of (dist, node); relax edges; skip stale entries.
Answer = max distance; unreachable nodes -> -1.
approach: Dijkstra from k; max of distances or -1.
complexity: Time O(e log n), Space O(n+e)

title: Alien Dictionary
statement: Derive the character order from a list of words sorted in an alien language.
hints: Compare adjacent words; first differing chars give an ordering edge.
Watch the invalid case: 'abc' before 'ab' is impossible.
Topological sort; a cycle means no valid order.
approach: Build graph from adjacent pairs; Kahn's sort; validate prefix case.

title: Redundant Connection
statement: A tree plus one extra edge; return the edge that can be removed to restore the tree.
hints: Process edges in order; the first edge joining two connected nodes is redundant.
Return the LAST such edge per the problem statement (with plain union-find it's the first found - re-read the spec).
Actually: return the edge that appears last in input among cycle-forming edges.
approach: Union-Find in input order; track the last cycle-forming edge.
pitfalls: Returning the first cycle edge instead of the last

title: Climbing Stairs
statement: Distinct ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps.
hints: Ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2): the last step is 1 or 2.
It's Fibonacci; two variables suffice.
Base: ways(1)=1, ways(2)=2.
approach: Iterative Fibonacci with O(1) space.

title: House Robber
statement: Max money robbing houses with no two adjacent.
hints: At each house: rob it (plus dp[i-2]) or skip it (dp[i-1]).
Two variables rolling forward.
Circular street: run twice, excluding first or last.
approach: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]).

title: Coin Change
statement: Fewest coins to make amount; -1 if impossible.
hints: dp[x] = 1 + min(dp[x - coin]) over coins; INF if unreachable.
Iterate amounts outer, coins inner (for min-coins formulation).
Greedy fails: coins [1,3,4], amount 6 -> greedy gives 4+1+1, optimal 3+3.
approach: Bottom-up DP over amounts with INF sentinel.
pitfalls: Wrong loop order confusion with counting variant

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
statement: Length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
hints: O(n^2): dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) for j < i with nums[j] < nums[i].
O(n log n): maintain tails[]; binary-search each number's position.
Tails isn't the subsequence - only its length is correct.
approach: Patience sorting with binary search on tails array.
complexity: Time O(n log n), Space O(n)

title: Word Break
statement: Can s be segmented into dictionary words?
hints: dp[i]: prefix of length i is segmentable.
For each i, try every j < i where dp[j] and s[j:i] in dict.
BFS/DFS with memo is equivalent.
approach: DP over prefix lengths with dictionary lookup.

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
statement: Can the array be split into two equal-sum subsets?
hints: Total must be even; then it's subset-sum to total/2.
1D boolean DP iterating sums BACKWARD (avoid reuse).
Classic 0/1 knapsack.
approach: Backward-iterating boolean DP for subset sum.

title: Decode Ways
statement: Number of ways to decode a digit string (1->A ... 26->Z).
hints: dp[i] += dp[i-1] if s[i-1] != '0'; dp[i] += dp[i-2] if 10 <= two-digit <= 26.
'0' is the trap: valid only inside 10 or 20.
Leading zeros make the answer 0 immediately.
approach: Linear DP with careful zero handling.

title: Unique Paths with Obstacles
statement: Count paths from top-left to bottom-right moving only down/right, avoiding obstacles.
hints: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]; obstacles force 0.
First row/col: 1s until the first obstacle.
In-place on the grid is fine.
approach: Grid DP with obstacle zeroing.

title: Edit Distance
statement: Minimum operations (insert, delete, replace) to convert word1 to word2.
hints: Define dp[i][j] on prefixes; consider the last characters.
If equal: dp[i-1][j-1]; else 1 + min(delete, insert, replace).
Base: converting to/from empty string costs the length.
approach: 2D DP over prefix pairs with the three-operation recurrence.
pitfalls: Forgetting replace as a distinct op

title: Longest Common Subsequence
statement: Length of the longest common subsequence of two strings.
hints: Match -> 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]; else max of skipping one char from either.
Backtrack through the table to reconstruct it.
Subsequence, not substring: gaps allowed.
approach: Classic 2D DP; optional reconstruction pass.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
statement: Maximum product of a contiguous subarray.
hints: Negatives flip: track BOTH max and min ending at each position.
On a negative, swap max and min before multiplying.
Kadane alone fails - why?
approach: Rolling max_ending/min_ending with swap on negatives.
pitfalls: Only tracking max (sign flips break it)

title: Jump Game II (min jumps)
statement: Minimum jumps to reach the end (each element = max jump length).
hints: Greedy layers: current jump's reach vs the farthest reachable.
When you exhaust the current range, jump and extend.
BFS-level thinking on an implicit graph.
approach: Greedy range expansion counting jumps.

title: Combination Sum
statement: All unique combinations summing to target; candidates reusable.
hints: Backtrack with a start index to avoid duplicate permutations.
Sort first so you can prune when the remainder goes negative.
Variants change the reuse/duplicate rules.
approach: DFS with start-index and pruning.
pitfalls: Permutations instead of combinations (no start index)

title: N-Queens II (count)
statement: Count distinct solutions to the n-queens puzzle.
hints: Place row by row; track attacked columns and diagonals in sets.
Diagonal ids: r+c and r-c are constant per diagonal.
Bitmask version is the optimized classic.
approach: Backtracking with column/diagonal sets.
pitfalls: Counting symmetric duplicates separately is fine

title: Regular Expression Matching
statement: Match string against pattern with '.' and '*' (zero or more of preceding).
hints: dp(i,j): does s[i:] match p[j:]? Handle '*' by zero-match (skip) or consume-one.
Memoize the recursion; base cases on empty pattern/string.
Draw the decision tree for 'a*' carefully.
approach: Memoized recursion on (i, j) with the star-branching rule.

title: Burst Balloons
statement: Max coins bursting balloons; bursting i yields nums[l]*nums[i]*nums[r].
hints: Think REVERSE: which balloon bursts LAST in interval (l, r)?
dp[l][r] = max over k of dp[l][k] + dp[k][r] + nums[l]*nums[k]*nums[r].
Pad with 1s at both ends.
approach: Interval DP over last-burst choice.

title: Binary Search (classic)
statement: Search a sorted array for target; return index or -1.
hints: Maintain [lo, hi]; mid = lo + (hi-lo)//2 avoids overflow.
Shrink the half that cannot contain the target.
Loop invariant: target in [lo, hi] if present.
approach: Iterative halving with overflow-safe midpoint.
pitfalls: Infinite loop from wrong bound updates

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
statement: Search target in a rotated sorted array.
hints: One half is always sorted - determine which via nums[lo] <= nums[mid].
Check if the target lies in the sorted half; else go to the other.
Duplicates break the worst case to O(n).
approach: Modified binary search using the sorted-half property.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
statement: Find the minimum element in a rotated sorted array.
hints: Compare nums[mid] with nums[hi] to decide the side.
The minimum is the only element smaller than its predecessor.
Duplicates: hi -= 1 fallback.
approach: Binary search toward the rotation pivot.

title: Koko Eating Bananas
statement: Minimum integer eating speed k to finish all piles within h hours.
hints: Binary search the ANSWER: speed in [1, max(piles)].
Feasibility: sum(ceil(pile / k)) <= h.
Monotonic: faster speeds only help.
approach: Binary search on speed with a feasibility check.
complexity: Time O(n log max), Space O(1)

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
statement: Median of two sorted arrays in O(log(m+n)).
hints: Binary search the partition: i + j = (m+n+1)//2 on the smaller array.
Valid when maxLeft1 <= minRight2 and maxLeft2 <= minRight1.
Handle empty partitions with infinities.
approach: Partition binary search; median from border values.

title: Search a 2D Matrix
statement: Matrix with rows sorted and first-of-row > last-of-previous; search target.
hints: Flatten conceptually: index i -> (i//n, i%n); binary search once.
Or staircase from top-right in O(m+n).
Compare the two approaches.
approach: Binary search on the virtual flat array.

title: Find Peak Element
statement: Find any peak (greater than neighbors) in O(log n).
hints: If nums[mid] < nums[mid+1], a peak must exist to the right.
The array edges act as -infinity.
Invariant: the chosen half always contains a peak.
approach: Binary search toward the rising slope.

title: Time Based Key-Value Store
statement: set(key, value, timestamp); get(key, timestamp) returns the latest value at or before timestamp.
hints: Per key, keep a list of (timestamp, value) in increasing order.
Binary search for the rightmost timestamp <= target.
Strictly increasing timestamps simplify appends.
approach: Hash map of sorted timestamp lists + binary search.
complexity: Time O(log n) get, Space O(n)
pitfalls: Leftmost vs rightmost binary search confusion

title: Sqrt(x) without built-ins
statement: Integer square root of x.
hints: Binary search answer in [0, x]; compare mid*mid with x.
Newton's method converges faster - mention it.
Avoid overflow: compare mid <= x // mid.
approach: Binary search on the answer range.

title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
statement: Minimum ship capacity to ship all weights within D days (order preserved).
hints: Binary search capacity in [max(weights), sum(weights)].
Feasibility: greedy day-packing count <= D.
Same answer-space pattern as Koko.
approach: Binary search on capacity with greedy feasibility.
complexity: Time O(n log sum), Space O(1)
pitfalls: Lower bound below max single weight

title: Find First and Last Position in Sorted Array
statement: Find the start/end indices of target in sorted array; [-1,-1] if absent.
hints: Two binary searches: lower bound and upper bound.
Or one search then expand - but that's O(n) worst case.
bisect_left / bisect_right model.
approach: Lower-bound and upper-bound binary searches.

title: Split Array Largest Sum
statement: Split into k subarrays minimizing the largest subarray sum.
hints: Binary search the answer: largest-sum in [max(nums), sum(nums)].
Feasibility: greedy counting of subarrays needed.
DP O(n^2 k) exists but binary search wins.
approach: Binary search on the minimized maximum with greedy check.
complexity: Time O(n log sum), Space O(1)
pitfalls: DP when constraints allow binary search

title: Two Sum (hashmap drill)
statement: Revisit Two Sum focusing on the hashmap pattern's generalizations.
hints: Complement lookup is the core pattern.
Same pattern: pair sums, difference k, subarray sums.
One pass vs two pass trade-offs.
approach: Single-pass complement map.

title: Group Anagrams (hashmap drill)
statement: Group strings by anagram equivalence using hashing.
hints: Canonical key per string: count-tuple is O(k).
Map key -> list; deterministic and fast.
Prime-product hashing is a fun alternative (overflow caveats).
approach: Count-tuple keys in a hash map.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
statement: Longest run of consecutive integers, O(n).
hints: Only start counting from sequence beginnings (x-1 not in set).
Each number is then visited at most twice overall.
Sorting is O(n log n) - beat it with a set.
approach: Hash set; expand only from sequence starts.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K (hashmap drill)
statement: Count subarrays summing to k via prefix sums.
hints: prefix[j] - prefix[i] = k -> need count of (prefix - k).
Seed {0: 1}; update after querying (order matters).
Works with negatives where sliding window fails.
approach: Running prefix with frequency map.

title: LRU Cache (hashmap + list drill)
statement: O(1) get/put cache with eviction.
hints: Map key -> node; doubly-linked list for recency order.
Dummy head/tail simplify edge cases.
OrderedDict is the library shortcut - implement manually first.
approach: Hash map + doubly linked list with dummies.
pitfalls: Singly linked list (can't evict in O(1))
Forgetting to update map on eviction

title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
statement: Set with O(1) insert, delete, and uniform random retrieval.
hints: Array for random access + map value -> index.
Delete by swapping with the last element.
Duplicates need index sets.
approach: Array + index map with swap-remove.

title: Design HashMap (from scratch)
statement: Implement a hash map with put/get/remove.
hints: Buckets array; chaining for collisions.
Hash function: built-in hash % capacity; handle negatives.
Resize when load factor exceeds ~0.75.
approach: Separate chaining with dynamic resize.

title: Word Pattern (bijection check)
statement: Check if a pattern string bijectively maps to words.
hints: Bijection needs BOTH directions checked.
Two maps, or one map + one set of used words.
Isomorphic Strings is the twin problem.
approach: Dual-direction mapping validation.

title: Reverse Integer (32-bit clamp)
statement: Reverse digits of a 32-bit signed integer; return 0 on overflow.
hints: Build the reversed number digit by digit.
Check overflow BEFORE multiplying: rev > INT_MAX//10 etc.
Python ints don't overflow - simulate the check anyway.
approach: Digit extraction loop with pre-overflow checks.

title: Pow(x, n) (fast exponentiation)
statement: Compute x^n in O(log n).
hints: x^n = (x^2)^(n/2); handle odd n with an extra multiply.
Negative n: invert x first.
Iterative bit-loop version too.
approach: Binary exponentiation, recursive or iterative.
complexity: Time O(log n), Space O(log n) / O(1)

title: Spiral Matrix
statement: Return matrix elements in spiral order.
hints: Shrink boundaries: top, bottom, left, right.
After each wall, check the loop condition again (single row/col left).
Direction arrays are an alternative.
approach: Boundary-shrinking traversal.
complexity: Time O(mn), Space O(1) excluding output

title: Rotate Image (90 degrees in place)
statement: Rotate an n x n matrix 90 degrees clockwise, in place.
hints: Transpose then reverse each row - two clean steps.
Or rotate 4-cycles layer by layer.
Verify on 3x3 by hand.
approach: Transpose + row reversal.

title: Set Matrix Zeroes (O(1) space)
statement: Zero out rows/columns containing a zero, constant space.
hints: Use the first row and column as marker storage.
Two flags remember whether the first row/col themselves need zeroing.
Mark first, then zero in a second pass.
approach: First-row/col markers + flags.

title: Game of Life (in-place)
statement: Next state of Conway's Game of Life, in place.
hints: Encode transitions in extra bits: 2 = dead->alive, 3 = alive->dead.
Count live neighbors using val % 2 (original state).
Second pass: shift right to finalize.
approach: In-place state encoding with bit tricks.
pitfalls: Counting transitional states as live/dead wrong

title: String to Integer (atoi)
statement: Parse a string to a 32-bit signed integer with clamping.
hints: Skip whitespace, read optional sign, then digits.
Clamp on overflow DURING parsing (pre-check).
Stop at the first non-digit.
approach: State-machine parse with overflow pre-checks.

title: Integer to Roman / Roman to Integer
statement: Convert between integers and Roman numerals.
hints: Greedy subtraction with value-symbol pairs including 4/9 forms (IV, IX...).
Reverse: add, but subtract when a smaller precedes a larger.
Table-driven is cleanest.
approach: Greedy table mapping both directions.

title: Multiply Strings (big integers as strings)
statement: Multiply two non-negative integer strings without big-int libs.
hints: Grade-school multiplication: result[i+j] += d1*d2, then carry.
Result has at most m+n digits.
Strip leading zeros.
approach: Positional accumulation + carry pass.

title: Plus One (digit array)
statement: Increment a large integer represented as a digit array.
hints: Add from the right with carry; early exit when no carry.
All 9s -> need a new leading 1.
The easy version of big-integer handling.
approach: Right-to-left increment with carry.

title: Happy Number (cycle detection)
statement: Determine if repeated digit-square-summing reaches 1.
hints: The sequence either reaches 1 or cycles - detect the cycle.
Floyd or a seen-set both work.
Why must it cycle? Values stay bounded.
approach: Cycle detection on the digit-square iteration.
complexity: Time O(log n) per step, Space O(1) Floyd

title: Excel Sheet Column Title/Number
statement: Convert between 1-indexed column numbers and titles (A..Z, AA...).
hints: It's base-26 but 1-indexed: no zero digit.
Number->title: (n-1) % 26 + 'A', then (n-1)//26.
Title->number: standard base-26 accumulation.
approach: Adjusted base-26 conversion both ways.
pitfalls: Plain base-26 (off by one on Z->AA)
